entries.48f7e6f34d9447f26075be18f648dac908f39316: <div sID="gen4563" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="24" osisID="Josh.24" sID="Josh.24"/> <div eID="gen4563" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4564" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen4565" type="x-p"/> This chapter concludes the life and reign of Joshua, in which we have, I. The great care and pains he took to confirm the people of Israel in the true faith and worship of God, that they might, after his death, persevere therein. In order to this he called another general assembly of the heads of the congregation of Israel (<reference osisRef="Josh.24.1">ver. 1</reference>) and dealt with them. 1. By way of narrative, recounting the great things God had done for them and their fathers, <reference osisRef="Josh.24.2-Josh.24.13">ver. 2-13</reference>. 2. By way of charge to them, in consideration thereof, to serve God, <reference osisRef="Josh.24.14">ver. 14</reference>. 3. By way of treaty with them, wherein he aims to bring them, (1.) To make religion their deliberate choice; and they did so, with reasons for their choice, <reference osisRef="Josh.24.15-Josh.24.18">ver. 15-18</reference>. (2.) To make it their determinate choice, and to resolve to adhere to it, <reference osisRef="Josh.24.19-Josh.24.24">ver. 19-24</reference>. 4. By way of covenant upon that treaty, <reference osisRef="Josh.24.25-Josh.24.28">ver. 25-28</reference>. II. The conclusion of this history, with, 1. The death and burial of Joshua (<reference osisRef="Josh.24.29-Josh.24.30">ver. 29, 30</reference>) and Eleazar (<reference osisRef="Josh.24.33">ver. 33</reference>), and the mention of the burial of Joseph's bones upon that occasion, <reference osisRef="Josh.24.32">ver. 32</reference>. 2. A general account of the state of Israel at that time, <reference osisRef="Josh.24.31">ver. 31</reference>.
entries.bbeb93326f666dc20e903aee2bbf4bfe2821f3cb: <div eID="gen4565" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Joshua's Farewell Address to Israel. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1427.)</title> <div sID="gen4566" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And Joshua gathered all the tribes of Israel to Shechem, and called for the elders of Israel, and for their heads, and for their judges, and for their officers; and they presented themselves before God. <hi type="super">2</hi> And Joshua said unto all the people, Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of Israel, Your fathers dwelt on the other side of the flood in old time, <hi type="italic">even</hi> Terah, the father of Abraham, and the father of Nachor: and they served other gods. <hi type="super">3</hi> And I took your father Abraham from the other side of the flood, and led him throughout all the land of Canaan, and multiplied his seed, and gave him Isaac. <hi type="super">4</hi> And I gave unto Isaac Jacob and Esau: and I gave unto Esau mount Seir, to possess it; but Jacob and his children went down into Egypt. <hi type="super">5</hi> I sent Moses also and Aaron, and I plagued Egypt, according to that which I did among them: and afterward I brought you out. <hi type="super">6</hi> And I brought your fathers out of Egypt: and ye came unto the sea; and the Egyptians pursued after your fathers with chariots and horsemen unto the Red sea. <hi type="super">7</hi> And when they cried unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , he put darkness between you and the Egyptians, and brought the sea upon them, and covered them; and your eyes have seen what I have done in Egypt: and ye dwelt in the wilderness a long season. <hi type="super">8</hi> And I brought you into the land of the Amorites, which dwelt on the other side Jordan; and they fought with you: and I gave them into your hand, that ye might possess their land; and I destroyed them from before you. <hi type="super">9</hi> Then Balak the son of Zippor, king of Moab, arose and warred against Israel, and sent and called Balaam the son of Beor to curse you: <hi type="super">10</hi> But I would not hearken unto Balaam; therefore he blessed you still: so I delivered you out of his hand. <hi type="super">11</hi> And ye went over Jordan, and came unto Jericho: and the men of Jericho fought against you, the Amorites, and the Perizzites, and the Canaanites, and the Hittites, and the Girgashites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites; and I delivered them into your hand. <hi type="super">12</hi> And I sent the hornet before you, which drave them out from before you, <hi type="italic">even</hi> the two kings of the Amorites; <hi type="italic">but</hi> not with thy sword, nor with thy bow. <hi type="super">13</hi> And I have given you a land for which ye did not labour, and cities which ye built not, and ye dwell in them; of the vineyards and oliveyards which ye planted not do ye eat. <hi type="super">14</hi> Now therefore fear the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and serve him in sincerity and in truth: and put away the gods which your fathers served on the other side of the flood, and in Egypt; and serve ye the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen4566" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4567" type="x-p"/> Joshua thought he had taken his last farewell of Israel in the solemn charge he gave them in the foregoing chapter, when he said, <hi type="italic">I go the way of all the earth;</hi> but God graciously continuing his life longer than expected, and renewing his strength, he was desirous to improve it for the good of Israel. He did not say, "I have taken my leave of them once, and let that serve;" but, having yet a longer space given him, he summons them together again, that he might try what more he could do to engage them for God. Note, We must never think our work for God done till our life is done; and, if he lengthen out our days beyond what we thought, we must conclude it is because he has some further service for us to do. <div eID="gen4567" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4568" type="x-p"/> The assembly is the same with that in the foregoing chapter, the <hi type="italic">elders, heads, judges, and officers of Israel,</hi> <reference osisRef="Josh.24.1">v. 1</reference>. But it is here made somewhat more solemn than it was there. <div eID="gen4568" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4569" type="x-p"/> I. The place appointed for their meeting is <hi type="italic">Shechem,</hi> not only because that lay nearer to Joshua than Shiloh, and therefore more convenient now that he was infirm and unfit for travelling, but because it was the place where Abraham, the first trustee of God's covenant with this people, settled at his coming to Canaan, and where God appeared to him (<reference osisRef="Gen.12.6-Gen.12.7">Gen. xii. 6, 7</reference>), and near which stood mounts Gerizim and Ebal, where the people had renewed their covenant with God at their first coming into Canaan, <reference osisRef="Josh.8.30">Josh. viii. 30</reference>. Of the promises God had made to their fathers, and of the promises they themselves had made to God, this place might serve to put them in mind. <div eID="gen4569" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4570" type="x-p"/> II. They presented themselves not only before Joshua, but before God, in this assembly, that is, they came together in a solemn religious manner, as into the special presence of God, and with an eye to his speaking to them by Joshua; and it is probable the service began with prayer. It is the conjecture of interpreters that upon this great occasion Joshua ordered the ark of God to be brought by the priests to Shechem, which, they say, was about ten miles from Shiloh, and to be set down in the place of their meeting, which is therefore called (<reference osisRef="Josh.24.26">v. 26</reference>) <hi type="italic">the sanctuary of the Lord,</hi> the presence of the ark making it so at that time; and this was done to grace the solemnity, and to strike an awe upon the people that attended. We have not now any such sensible tokens of the divine presence, but are to believe that <hi type="italic">where two or three are gathered together</hi> in Christ's name he is as really in the midst of them as God was where the ark was, and they are indeed presenting themselves before him. <div eID="gen4570" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4571" type="x-p"/> III. Joshua spoke to them in God's name, and as from him, in the language of a prophet (<reference osisRef="Josh.24.2">v. 2</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Thus saith the Lord,</hi> Jehovah, the great God, and the God of Israel, your God in covenant, whom therefore you are bound to hear and give heed to." Note, The word of God is to be received by us as his, whoever is the messenger that brings it, whose greatness cannot add to it, nor his meanness diminish from it. His sermon consists of doctrine and application. <div eID="gen4571" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4572" type="x-p"/> 1. The doctrinal part is a history of the great things God had done for his people, and for their fathers before them. God by Joshua recounts the marvels of old: "I did so and so." They must know and consider, not only that such and such things were done, but that God did them. It is a series of wonders that is here recorded, and perhaps many more were mentioned by Joshua, which for brevity's sake are here omitted. See what God had wrought. (1.) He brought Abraham out of Ur of the Chaldees, <reference osisRef="Josh.24.2-Josh.24.3">v. 2, 3</reference>. He and his ancestors had served other gods there, for it was the country in which, though celebrated for learning, idolatry, as some think, had its rise; there <hi type="italic">the world by wisdom knew not God.</hi> Abraham, who afterwards was the friend of God and the great favourite of heaven, was bred up in idolatry, and lived long in it, till God by his grace snatched him as a brand out of that burning. Let them remember that rock out of which they were hewn, and not relapse into that sin from which their fathers by a miracle of free grace were delivered. "I took him," says God, "else he had never come out of that sinful state." Hence Abraham's justification is made by the apostle an instance of God's <hi type="italic">justifying the ungodly,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.4.5">Rom. iv. 5</reference>. (2.) He brought him to Canaan, and built up his family, led him through the land to Shechem, where they now were, multiplied his seed by Ishmael, who begat twelve princes, but at last gave him Isaac the promised son, and in him multiplied his seed. When Isaac had two sons, Jacob and Esau, God provided an inheritance for Esau elsewhere in Mount Seir, that the land of Canaan might be reserved entire for the seed of Jacob, and the posterity of Esau might not pretend to a share in it. (3.) He delivered the seed of Jacob out of Egypt with a high hand (<reference osisRef="Josh.24.5-Josh.24.6">v. 5, 6</reference>), and rescued them out of the hands of Pharaoh and his host at the Red Sea, <reference osisRef="Josh.24.6-Josh.24.7">v. 6, 7</reference>. The same waters were the Israelites' guard and the Egyptians' grave, and this in answer to prayer; for, though we find in the story that they in that distress murmured against God (<reference osisRef="Exod.14.11-Exod.14.12">Exod. xiv. 11, 12</reference>), notice is here taken of their <hi type="italic">crying to God;</hi> he graciously accepted those that prayed to him, and overlooked the folly of those that quarrelled with him. (4.) He protected them in the wilderness, where they are here said, not to <hi type="italic">wander,</hi> but to <hi type="italic">dwell for a long season,</hi> <reference osisRef="Josh.24.7">v. 7</reference>. So wisely were all their motions directed, and so safely were they kept, that even there they had as certain a dwelling-place as if they had been in a walled city. (5.) He gave them the land of the Amorites, on the other side Jordan (<reference osisRef="Josh.24.8">v. 8</reference>), and there defeated the plot of Balak and Balaam against them, so that Balaam could not curse them as he desired, and therefore Balak durst not fight them as he designed, and as, because he designed it, he is here said to have done it. The turning of Balaam's tongue to bless Israel, when he intended to curse them, is often mentioned as an instance of the divine power put forth in Israel's favour as remarkable as any, because in it God proved (and does still, more than we are aware of) his dominion over the powers of darkness, and over the spirits of men. (6.) He brought them safely and triumphantly into Canaan, delivered the Canaanites into their hand (<reference osisRef="Josh.24.11">v. 11</reference>), <hi type="italic">sent hornets before them,</hi> when they were actually engaged in battle with the enemy, which with their stings tormented them and with their noise terrified them, so that they became a very easy prey to Israel. These dreadful swarms first appeared in their war with Sihon and Og, the two kings of the Amorites, and afterwards in their other battles, <reference osisRef="Josh.24.12">v. 12</reference>. God had promised to do this for them, <reference osisRef="Exod.23.27-Exod.23.28">Exod. xxiii. 27, 28</reference>. And here Joshua takes notice of the fulfilling of that promise. See <reference osisRef="Exod.23.27-Exod.23.28">Exod. xxiii. 27, 28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.7.20">Deut. vii. 20</reference>. These hornets, it should seem, annoyed the enemy more than the artillery of Israel, and therefore he adds, <hi type="italic">not with thy sword nor bow.</hi> It was purely the Lord's doing. <hi type="italic">Lastly,</hi> They were now in the peaceable possession of a good land, and lived comfortably upon the fruit of other people's labours, <reference osisRef="Josh.24.13">v. 13</reference>. <div eID="gen4572" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4573" type="x-p"/> 2. The application of this history of God's mercies to them is by way of exhortation to fear and serve God, in gratitude for his favour, and that it might be continued to them, <reference osisRef="Josh.24.14">v. 14</reference>. Now therefore, in consideration of all this, (1.) "<hi type="italic">Fear the Lord,</hi> the Lord and his goodness, <reference osisRef="Hos.3.5">Hos. iii. 5</reference>. Reverence a God of such infinite power, fear to offend him and to forfeit his goodness, keep up an awe of his majesty, a deference to his authority, a dread of his displeasure, and a continual regard to his all-seeing eye upon you." (2.) "Let your practice be consonant to this principle, and serve him both by the outward acts of religious worship and every instance of obedience in your whole conversation, and this <hi type="italic">in sincerity and truth,</hi> with a single eye and an upright heart, and inward impressions answerable to outward expressions." This is the <hi type="italic">truth in the inward part,</hi> which God requires, <reference osisRef="Ps.51.6">Ps. li. 6</reference>. For what good will it do us to dissemble with a God that searches the heart? (3.) <hi type="italic">Put away the strange gods,</hi> both Chaldean and Egyptian idols, for those they were most in danger of revolting to. It should seem by this charge, which is repeated (<reference osisRef="Josh.24.23">v. 23</reference>), that there were some among them that privately kept in their closets the images or pictures of these dunghill-deities, which came to their hands from their ancestors, as heir-looms of their families, though, it may be, they did not worship them; these Joshua earnestly urges them to throw away: "Deface them, destroy them, lest you be tempted to serve them." Jacob pressed his household to do this, and at this very place; for, when they gave him up the little images they had, he buried them <hi type="italic">under the oak which was by Shechem,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.35.2">Gen. xxxv. 2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.35.4">4</reference>. Perhaps the oak mentioned here (<reference osisRef="Josh.24.26">v. 26</reference>) was the same oak, or another in the same place, which might be well called the <hi type="italic">oak of reformation,</hi> as there were idolatrous oaks.
entries.e47ea4992a646d737c800a74c83ddae86d924d8f: <div eID="gen4573" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4574" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> And if it seem evil unto you to serve the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , choose you this day whom ye will serve; whether the gods which your fathers served that <hi type="italic">were</hi> on the other side of the flood, or the gods of the Amorites, in whose land ye dwell: but as for me and my house, we will serve the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">16</hi> And the people answered and said, God forbid that we should forsake the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , to serve other gods; <hi type="super">17</hi> For the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> our God, he <hi type="italic">it is</hi> that brought us up and our fathers out of the land of Egypt, from the house of bondage, and which did those great signs in our sight, and preserved us in all the way wherein we went, and among all the people through whom we passed: <hi type="super">18</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> drave out from before us all the people, even the Amorites which dwelt in the land: <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> will we also serve the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; for he <hi type="italic">is</hi> our God. <hi type="super">19</hi> And Joshua said unto the people, Ye cannot serve the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : for he <hi type="italic">is</hi> a holy God; he <hi type="italic">is</hi> a jealous God; he will not forgive your transgressions nor your sins. <hi type="super">20</hi> If ye forsake the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and serve strange gods, then he will turn and do you hurt, and consume you, after that he hath done you good. <hi type="super">21</hi> And the people said unto Joshua, Nay; but we will serve the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">22</hi> And Joshua said unto the people, Ye <hi type="italic">are</hi> witnesses against yourselves that ye have chosen you the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , to serve him. And they said, <hi type="italic">We are</hi> witnesses. <hi type="super">23</hi> Now therefore put away, <hi type="italic">said he,</hi> the strange gods which <hi type="italic">are</hi> among you, and incline your heart unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of Israel. <hi type="super">24</hi> And the people said unto Joshua, The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> our God will we serve, and his voice will we obey. <hi type="super">25</hi> So Joshua made a covenant with the people that day, and set them a statute and an ordinance in Shechem. <hi type="super">26</hi> And Joshua wrote these words in the book of the law of God, and took a great stone, and set it up there under an oak, that <hi type="italic">was</hi> by the sanctuary of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">27</hi> And Joshua said unto all the people, Behold, this stone shall be a witness unto us; for it hath heard all the words of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> which he spake unto us: it shall be therefore a witness unto you, lest ye deny your God. <hi type="super">28</hi> So Joshua let the people depart, every man unto his inheritance. <div eID="gen4574" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4575" type="x-p"/> Never was any treaty carried on with better management, nor brought to a better issue, than this of Joshua with the people, to engage them to serve God. The manner of his dealing with them shows him to have been in earnest, and that his heart was much upon it, to leave them under all possible obligations to cleave to him, particularly the obligation of a choice and of a covenant. <div eID="gen4575" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4576" type="x-p"/> I. Would it be any obligation upon them if they made the service of God their choice?—he here puts them to their choice, not as if it were antecedently indifferent whether they served God or nor, or as if they were at liberty to refuse his service, but because it would have a great influence upon their perseverance in religion if they embraced it with the reason of men and with the resolution of men. These two things he here brings them to. <div eID="gen4576" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4577" type="x-p"/> 1. He brings them to embrace their religion rationally and intelligently, for it is a reasonable service. The will of man is apt to glory in its native liberty, and, in a jealousy for the honour of this, adheres with most pleasure to that which is its own choice and is not imposed upon it; therefore it is God's will that this service should be, not our chance, or a force upon us, but our choice. Accordingly, <div eID="gen4577" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4578" type="x-p"/> (1.) Joshua fairly puts the matter to their choice, <reference osisRef="Josh.24.15">v. 15</reference>. Here, [1.] He proposes the candidates that stand for the election. The Lord, Jehovah, on one side, and on the other side either the gods of their ancestors, which would pretend to recommend themselves to those that were fond of antiquity, and that which was received by tradition from their fathers, or the <hi type="italic">gods of their neighbours,</hi> the Amorites, in <hi type="italic">whose land they dwelt,</hi> which would insinuate themselves into the affections of those that were complaisant and fond of good fellowship. [2.] He supposes there were those to whom, upon some account or other, it would <hi type="italic">seem evil to serve the Lord.</hi> There are prejudices and objections which some people raise against religion, which, with those that are inclined to the world and the flesh, have great force. It seems evil to them, hard and unreasonable, to be obliged to deny themselves, mortify the flesh, take up their cross, &c. But, being in a state of probation, it is fit there should be some difficulties in the way, else there were no trial. [3.] He refers it to themselves: "<hi type="italic">Choose you whom you will serve,</hi> choose this day, now that the matter is laid thus plainly before you, speedily bring it to a head, and do not stand hesitating." Elijah, long after this, referred the decision of the controversy between Jehovah and Baal to the consciences of those with whom he was treating, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.21">1 Kings xviii. 21</reference>. Joshua's putting the matter here to this issue plainly intimates two things:—<hi type="italic">First,</hi> That it is the will of God we should every one of us make religion our serious and deliberate choice. Let us state the matter impartially to ourselves, weigh things in an even balance, and then determine for that which we find to be really true and good. Let us resolve upon a life of serious godliness, not merely because we know no other way, but because really, upon search, we find no better. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> That religion has so much self-evident reason and righteousness on its side that it may safely be referred to every man that allows himself a free thought either to choose or refuse it; for the merits of the cause are so plain that no considerate man can do otherwise but choose it. The case is so clear that it determines itself. Perhaps Joshua designed, by putting them to their choice, thus to try if there were any among them who, upon so fair an occasion given, would show a coolness and indifference towards the service of God, whether they would desire time to consider and consult their friends before they gave in an answer, and if any such should appear he might set a mark upon them, and warn the rest to avoid them. [4.] He directs their choice in this matter by an open declaration of his own resolutions: "<hi type="italic">But as for me and my house,</hi> whatever you do, <hi type="italic">we will serve the Lord,</hi> and I hope you will all be of the same mind." Here he resolves, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> For himself: <hi type="italic">As for me, I will serve the Lord.</hi> Note, The service of God is nothing below the greatest of men; it is so far from being a diminution and disparagement to princes and those of the first rank to be religious that it is their greatest honour, and adds the brightest crown of glory to them. Observe how positive he is: "I will serve God." It is no abridgment of our liberty to bind ourselves with a bond to God. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> For <hi type="italic">his house,</hi> that is, his family, his children and servants, such as were immediately under his eye and care, his inspection and influence. Joshua was a ruler, a judge in Israel, yet he did not make his necessary application to public affairs an excuse for the neglect of family religion. Those that have the charge of many families, as magistrates and ministers, must take special care of their own (<reference osisRef="1Tim.3.4-1Tim.3.5">1 Tim. iii. 4, 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">I and my house</hi> will serve God. 1. "Not my house, without me." He would not engage them to that work which he would not set his own hand to. As some who would have their children and servants good, but will not be so themselves; that is, they would have them go to heaven, but intend to go to hell themselves. 2. "Not I, without my house." He supposes he might be forsaken by his people, but in his house, where his authority was greater and more immediate, there he would over-rule. Note, When we cannot bring as many as we would to the service of God we must bring as many as we can, and extend our endeavours to the utmost sphere of our activity; if we cannot reform the land, let us put away iniquity far from our own tabernacle. 3. "First I, and then my house." Note, Those that lead and rule in other things should be first in the service of God, and go before in the best things. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> He resolves to do this whatever others did. Though all the families of Israel should revolt from God, and serve idols, yet Joshua and his family will stedfastly adhere to the God of Israel. Note, Those that resolve to serve God must not mind being singular in it, nor be drawn by the crowd to forsake his service. Those that are bound for heaven must be willing to swim against the stream, and must not do as the most do, but as the best do. <div eID="gen4578" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4579" type="x-p"/> (2.) The matter being thus put to their choice, they immediately determine it by a free, rational, and intelligent declaration, for the God of Israel, against all competitors whatsoever, <reference osisRef="Josh.24.16-Josh.24.18">v. 16-18</reference>. Here, [1.] They concur with Joshua in his resolution, being influenced by the example of so great a man, who had been so great a blessing to them (<reference osisRef="Josh.24.18">v. 18</reference>): <hi type="italic">We also will serve the Lord.</hi> See how much good great men might do, if they were but zealous in religion, by their influence on their inferiors. [2.] They startle at the thought of apostatizing from God (<reference osisRef="Josh.24.16">v. 16</reference>): <hi type="italic">God forbid;</hi> the word intimates the greatest dread and detestation imaginable. "Far be it, far be it from us, that we or ours should ever <hi type="italic">forsake the Lord to serve other gods.</hi> We must be perfectly lost to all sense of justice, gratitude, and honour, ere we can harbour the least thought of such a thing." Thus must our hearts rise against all temptations to desert the service of God. <hi type="italic">Get thee behind me, Satan.</hi> [3.] They give very substantial reasons for their choice, to show that they did not make it purely in compliance to Joshua, but from a full conviction of the reasonableness and equity of it. They make this choice for, and in consideration, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Of the many great and very kind things God had done for them, bringing them out of Egypt through the wilderness into Canaan, <reference osisRef="Josh.24.17-Josh.24.18">v. 17, 18</reference>. Thus they repeat to themselves Joshua's sermon, and then express their sincere compliance with the intentions of it. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Of the relation they stood in to God, and his covenant with them: "We <hi type="italic">will serve the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="Josh.24.18">v. 18</reference>), <hi type="italic">for he is our God,</hi> who has graciously engaged himself by promise to us, and to whom we have by solemn vow engaged ourselves." <div eID="gen4579" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4580" type="x-p"/> 2. He brings them to embrace their religion resolutely, and to express a full purpose of heart to cleave to the Lord. Now that he has them in a good mind he follows his blow, and drives the nail to the head, that it might, if possible, be a nail in a sure place. Fast bind, fast find. <div eID="gen4580" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4581" type="x-p"/> (1.) In order to this he sets before them the difficulties of religion, and that in it which might be thought discouraging (<reference osisRef="Josh.24.19-Josh.24.20">v. 19, 20</reference>): <hi type="italic">You cannot serve the Lord, for he is a holy God,</hi> or, as it is in the Hebrew, <hi type="italic">he is the holy Gods,</hi> intimating the mystery of the Trinity, three in one; <hi type="italic">holy, holy, holy,</hi> holy Father, holy Son, holy Spirit. <hi type="italic">He will not forgive.</hi> And, <hi type="italic">if you forsake him, he will do you hurt.</hi> Certainly Joshua does not intend hereby to deter them from the service of God as impracticable and dangerous. But, [1.] He perhaps intends to represent here the suggestions of seducers, who tempted Israel from their God, and from the service of him; with such insinuations as these, that he was a hard master, his work impossible to be done, and he not to be pleased, and, if displeased, implacable and revengeful,—that he would confine their respects to himself only, and would not suffer them to show the least kindness for any other,—and that herein he was very unlike the gods of the nations, which were easy, and neither holy nor jealous. It is probable that this was then commonly objected against the Jewish religion, as it has all along been the artifice of Satan every since he tempted our first parents thus to misrepresent God and his laws, as harsh and severe; and Joshua by his tone and manner of speaking might make them perceive he intended it as an objection, and would put it to them how they would keep their ground against the force of it. Or, [2.] He thus expresses his godly jealousy over them, and his fear concerning them, that, notwithstanding the profession they now made of zeal for God and his service, they would afterwards draw back, and if they did they would find him just and jealous to avenge it. Or, [3.] He resolves to let them know the worst of it, and what strict terms they must expect to stand upon with God, that they might sit down and count the cost. "<hi type="italic">You cannot serve the Lord,</hi> except you put away all other gods for he is holy and jealous, and will by no means admit a rival, and therefore you must be very watchful and careful, for it is at your peril if you desert his service; better you had never known it." Thus, though our Master has assured us that <hi type="italic">his yoke is easy,</hi> yet lest, upon the presumption of this, we should grow remiss and careless, he has also told us that the gate is strait, and the way narrow, that leads to life, that we may therefore strive to enter, and not seek only. "<hi type="italic">You cannot serve God and Mammon;</hi> therefore, if you resolve to serve God, you must renounce all competitors with him. You cannot serve God in your own strength, nor will he forgive your transgressions for any righteousness of your own; but <hi type="italic">all the seed of Israel must be justified and must glory in the Lord alone as their righteousness</hi> and <hi type="italic">strength,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Isa.45.24-Isa.45.25">Isa. xlv. 24, 25</reference>. They must therefore come off from all confidence in their own sufficiency, else their purposes would be to no purpose. Or, [4.] Joshua thus urges on them the seeming discouragements which lay in their way, that he might sharpen their resolutions, and draw from them a promise yet more express and solemn that they would continue faithful to God and their religion. He draws it from them that they might catch at it the more earnestly and hold it the faster. <div eID="gen4581" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4582" type="x-p"/> (2.) Notwithstanding this statement of the difficulties of religion, they declare a firm and fixed resolution to continue and persevere therein (<reference osisRef="Josh.24.21">v. 21</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Nay, but we will serve the Lord.</hi> We will think never the worse of him for his being a holy and jealous God, nor for his confining his servants to worship himself only. Justly will he consume those that forsake him, but we never will forsake him; not only we have a good mind to serve him, and we hope we shall, but we are at a point, we cannot bear to hear any <hi type="italic">entreaties to leave him or to turn from following after him</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ruth.1.16">Ruth i. 16</reference>); in the strength of divine grace we are resolved that we will serve the Lord." This resolution they repeat with an explication (<reference osisRef="Josh.24.24">v. 24</reference>): "<hi type="italic">The Lord our God will we serve,</hi> not only be called his servants and wear his livery, but our religion shall rule us in every thing, <hi type="italic">and his voice will we obey.</hi>" And in vain do we <hi type="italic">call him Master and Lord, if we do not the things which he saith,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.6.46">Luke vi. 46</reference>. This last promise they make in answer to the charge Joshua gave them (<reference osisRef="Josh.24.23">v. 23</reference>), that, in order to their perseverance, they should, [1.] Put away the images and relics of the strange gods, and not keep any of the tokens of those other lovers in their custody, if they resolved their <hi type="italic">Maker should be their husband;</hi> they promise, in this, to obey his voice. [2.] That they should <hi type="italic">incline their hearts to the God of Israel,</hi> use their authority over their own hearts to engage them for God, not only to set their affections upon him, but to settle them so. These terms they agree to, and thus, as Joshua explains the bargain, they strike it: <hi type="italic">The Lord our God will we serve.</hi> <div eID="gen4582" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4583" type="x-p"/> II. The service of God being thus made their deliberate choice, Joshua binds them to it by a solemn covenant, <reference osisRef="Josh.24.25">v. 25</reference>. Moses had twice publicly ratified this covenant between God and Israel, at Mount Sinai (<reference osisRef="Exod.24.1-Exod.24.33">Exod. xxiv.</reference>) and in the plains of Moab, <reference osisRef="Deut.29.1">Deut. xxix. 1</reference>. Joshua had likewise done it once (<reference osisRef="Josh.8.31-Josh.8.35">ch. viii. 31</reference>, &c.) and now the second time. It is here called a <hi type="italic">statute</hi> and an <hi type="italic">ordinance,</hi> because of the strength and perpetuity of its obligation, and because even this covenant bound them to no more than what they were antecedently bound to by the divine command. Now, to give it the formalities of a covenant, 1. He calls witnesses, no other than themselves (<reference osisRef="Josh.24.22">v. 22</reference>): <hi type="italic">You are witnesses that you have chosen the Lord.</hi> He promises himself that they would never forget the solemnities of this day; but, if hereafter they should break this covenant, he assures them that the professions and promises they had now made would certainly rise up in judgment against them and condemn them; and they agreed to it: "<hi type="italic">We are witnesses;</hi> let us be judged out of our own mouths if ever we be false to our God." 2. He put it in writing, and inserted it, as we find it here, in the sacred canon: He <hi type="italic">wrote it in the book of the law</hi> (<reference osisRef="Josh.24.26">v. 26</reference>), in that original which was laid up in the side of the ark, and thence, probably, it was transcribed into the several copies which the princes had for the use of each tribe. There it was written, that their obligation to religion by the divine precept, and that by their own promise, might remain on record together. 3. He erected a memorandum of it, for the benefit of those who perhaps were not conversant with writings, <reference osisRef="Josh.24.26-Josh.24.27">v. 26, 27</reference>. He <hi type="italic">set up a great stone under an oak,</hi> as a monument of this covenant, and perhaps wrote an inscription upon it (by which stones are made to speak) signifying the intention of it. When he says, <hi type="italic">It hath heard</hi> what was past, he tacitly upbraids the people with the hardness of their hearts, as if this stone had heard to as good purpose as some of them; and, if they should forget what was no done, this stone would so far preserve the remembrance of it as to reproach them for their stupidity and carelessness, and be a witness against them. <div eID="gen4583" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4584" type="x-p"/> The matter being thus settled, Joshua dismissed this assembly of the grandees of Israel (<reference osisRef="Josh.24.28">v. 28</reference>), and took his last leave of them, well satisfied in having done his part, by which he had delivered his soul; if they perished, their blood would be upon their own heads.
entries.bb603286e9a495d89d917bd82980a3c4d9ff659c: <div eID="gen4584" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Death of Joshua. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1427.)</title> <div sID="gen4585" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">29</hi> And it came to pass after these things, that Joshua the son of Nun, the servant of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , died, <hi type="italic">being</hi> a hundred and ten years old. <hi type="super">30</hi> And they buried him in the border of his inheritance in Timnath-serah, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> in mount Ephraim, on the north side of the hill of Gaash. <hi type="super">31</hi> And Israel served the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> all the days of Joshua, and all the days of the elders that overlived Joshua, and which had known all the works of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , that he had done for Israel. <hi type="super">32</hi> And the bones of Joseph, which the children of Israel brought up out of Egypt, buried they in Shechem, in a parcel of ground which Jacob bought of the sons of Hamor the father of Shechem for a hundred pieces of silver: and it became the inheritance of the children of Joseph. <hi type="super">33</hi> And Eleazar the son of Aaron died; and they buried him in a hill <hi type="italic">that pertained to</hi> Phinehas his son, which was given him in mount Ephraim. <div eID="gen4585" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4586" type="x-p"/> This book, which began with triumphs, here ends with funerals, by which all the glory of man is stained. We have here 1. The burial of Joseph, <reference osisRef="Josh.24.32">v. 32</reference>. He died about 200 years before in Egypt, but <hi type="italic">gave commandment concerning his bones,</hi> that they should not rest in their grave until Israel had rest in the land of promise; now therefore the children of Israel, who had brought this coffin full of bones with them out of Egypt, carried it along with them in all their marches through the wilderness (the two tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh, it is probable, taking particular care of it), and kept it in their camp till Canaan was perfectly reduced, now at last they deposited it in that piece of ground which his father gave him near Shechem, <reference osisRef="Gen.48.22">Gen. xlviii. 22</reference>. Probably it was upon this occasion that Joshua called for all Israel to meet him at Shechem (<reference osisRef="Josh.24.1">v. 1</reference>), to attend Joseph's coffin to the grave there, so that the sermon in this chapter served both for Joseph's funeral sermon and his own farewell sermon; and if it was, as is supposed, in the last year of his life, the occasion might very well remind him of his own death being at hand, for he was not just at the same age that his illustrious ancestor Joseph had arrived at when he died, 110 <hi type="italic">years old;</hi> compare <reference osisRef="Josh.24.29">v. 29</reference> with <reference osisRef="Gen.50.26">Gen. l. 26</reference>. 2. The death and burial of Joshua, <reference osisRef="Josh.24.29-Josh.24.30">v. 29, 30</reference>. We are not told how long he lived after the coming of Israel into Canaan. Dr. Lightfoot thinks it was about seventeen years; but the Jewish chronologers generally say it was about twenty-seven or twenty-eight years. He is here called the <hi type="italic">servant of the Lord,</hi> the same title that was given to Moses (<reference osisRef="Josh.1.1">ch. i. 1</reference>) when mention was made of his death; for, though Joshua was in many respects inferior to Moses, yet in this he was equal to him, that, according as his work was, he approved himself a diligent and faithful servant of God. And he that traded with his two talents had the same approbation that he had who traded with his five. <hi type="italic">Well done, good and faithful servant.</hi> Joshua's burying-place is here said to be <hi type="italic">on the north side of the hill Gaash,</hi> or <hi type="italic">the quaking hill;</hi> the Jews say it was so called because it trembled at the burial of Joshua, to upbraid the people of Israel with their stupidity in that they did not lament the death of that great and good man as they ought to have done. Thus at the death of Christ, our Joshua, the earth quaked. The learned bishop Patrick observes that there is no mention of any days of mourning being observed for Joshua, as there were for Moses and Aaron, in which, he says, St. Hierom and others of the fathers think there is a mystery, namely, that under the law, when life and immortality were not brought to so clear a light as they are now, they had reason to mourn and weep for the death of their friends; but now that Jesus, our Joshua, has opened the kingdom of heaven, we may rather rejoice. 3. The death and burial of Eleazar the chief priest, who, it is probable, died about the same time that Joshua did, as Aaron in the same year with Moses, <reference osisRef="Josh.24.33">v. 33</reference>. The Jews say that Eleazar, a little before he died, called the elders together, and gave them a charge as Joshua had done. He was buried in a hill that pertained to Phinehas his son, which came to him, not by descent, for then it would have pertained to his father first, nor had the priests any cities in Mount Ephraim, but either it fell to him by marriage, as the Jews conjecture, or it was freely bestowed upon him, to build a country seat on, by some pious Israelite that was well-affected to the priesthood, for it is here said to have been <hi type="italic">given him;</hi> and there he buried his dear father. 4. A general idea given us of the state of Israel at this time, <reference osisRef="Josh.24.31">v. 31</reference>. While Joshua lived, religion was kept up among them under his care and influence; but soon after he and his contemporaries died it went to decay, so much oftentimes does one head hold up: how well is it for the gospel church that Christ, our Joshua, is still with it, by his Spirit, and will be always, even <hi type="italic">unto the end of the world!</hi>  <div eID="gen4586" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen4564" type="introduction"/> <chapter eID="Josh.24"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen4070" osisID="Josh" type="book"/>

entries.008291b38730ffb43e36d97f9ae2cd7cc7b4069f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2186"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 24</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Josh.24.1">Jos 24:1</reference>. Joshua Assembling the Tribes.</title> <div sID="gen2934" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2186"/><hi type="bold">1. Joshua gathered all the tribes of Israel to Shechem--</hi>Another and final opportunity of dissuading the people against idolatry is here described as taken by the aged leader, whose solicitude on this account arose from his knowledge of the extreme readiness of the people to conform to the manners of the surrounding nations. This address was made to the representatives of the people convened at Shechem, and which had already been the scene of a solemn renewal of the covenant (<reference osisRef="Josh.8.30">Jos 8:30</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.8.35">35</reference>). The transaction now to be entered upon being in principle and object the same, it was desirable to give it all the solemn impressiveness which might be derived from the memory of the former ceremonial, as well as from other sacred associations of the place (<reference osisRef="Gen.12.6">Ge 12:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.12.7">7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.33.18-Gen.33.20">33:18-20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.35.2-Gen.35.4">35:2-4</reference>).<div eID="gen2934" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2935" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they presented themselves before God--</hi>It is generally assumed that the ark of the covenant had been transferred on this occasion to Shechem; as on extraordinary emergencies it was for a time removed (<reference osisRef="Judg.20.1-Judg.20.18">Jud 20:1-18</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.4.3">1Sa 4:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.24">2Sa 15:24</reference>). But the statement, not necessarily implying this, may be viewed as expressing only the religious character of the ceremony [Hengstenberg]. <div eID="gen2935" type="x-p"/>
entries.3128fe3fb137316433f6933d509742e0adcfee07: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2187"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Josh.24.2-Josh.24.13">Jos 24:2-13</reference>. Relates God's Benefits.</title> <div sID="gen2936" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2187"/><hi type="bold">2. Joshua said unto all the people--</hi>His address briefly recapitulated the principal proofs of the divine goodness to Israel from the call of Abraham to their happy establishment in the land of promise; it showed them that they were indebted for their national existence as well as their peculiar privileges, not to any merits of their own, but to the free grace of God.<div eID="gen2936" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2937" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Your fathers dwelt on the other side of the flood--</hi>The Euphrates, namely, at Ur.<div eID="gen2937" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2938" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Terah, the father of Abraham, and the father of Nachor--</hi>(see <reference osisRef="Gen.11.27">Ge 11:27</reference>). Though Terah had three sons, Nahor only is mentioned with Abraham, as the Israelites were descended from him on the mother's side through Rebekah and her nieces, Leah and Rachel.<div eID="gen2938" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2939" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">served other gods--</hi>conjoining, like Laban, the traditional knowledge of the true God with the domestic use of material images (<reference osisRef="Gen.31.19">Ge 31:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.31.34">34</reference>). <div eID="gen2939" type="x-p"/>
entries.3d5e65232b0b5fa38544f046cd6e6dbf0510db13: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2188"/><div sID="gen2940" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2188"/><hi type="bold">3. I took your father Abraham from the other side of the flood, and led him throughout all the land of Canaan--</hi>It was an irresistible impulse of divine grace which led the patriarch to leave his country and relatives, to migrate to Canaan, and live a "stranger and pilgrim" in that land. <div eID="gen2940" type="x-p"/>
entries.8291e76c710e6d6f256f655d11cddcee911bb75b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2189"/><div sID="gen2941" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2189"/><hi type="bold">4. I gave unto Esau mount Seir--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Gen.36.8">Ge 36:8</reference>). In order that he might be no obstacle to Jacob and his posterity being the exclusive heirs of Canaan. <div eID="gen2941" type="x-p"/>
entries.f575eb012367e92539d795720308b07c1be6ab24: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2190"/><div sID="gen2942" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2190"/><hi type="bold">12. I sent the hornet before you--</hi>a particular species of wasp which swarms in warm countries and sometimes assumes the scourging character of a plague; or, as many think, it is a figurative expression for uncontrollable terror (see on <reference osisRef="Exod.23.28">Ex 23:28</reference>). <div eID="gen2942" type="x-p"/>
entries.28b766a128a9385a544404b9d243719ac4d7e2ac: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2191"/><div sID="gen2943" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2191"/><hi type="bold">14-28. Now therefore fear the Lord, and serve him in sincerity and in truth--</hi>After having enumerated so many grounds for national gratitude, Joshua calls on them to declare, in a public and solemn manner, whether they will be faithful and obedient to the God of Israel. He avowed this to be his own unalterable resolution, and urged them, if they were sincere in making a similar avowal, "to put away the strange gods that were among them"--a requirement which seems to imply that some were suspected of a strong hankering for, or concealed practice of, the idolatry, whether in the form of Zabaism, the fire-worship of their Chaldean ancestors, or the grosser superstitions of the Canaanites. <div eID="gen2943" type="x-p"/>
entries.7f72c1c9a9323a37eb79c8278de06777f30f1406: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2193"/><div sID="gen2949" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2193"/><hi type="bold">29-30. Joshua ... died--</hi>Lightfoot computes that he lived seventeen, others twenty-seven years, after the entrance into Canaan. He was buried, according to the Jewish practice, within the limits of his own inheritance. The eminent public services he had long rendered to Israel and the great amount of domestic comfort and national prosperity he had been instrumental in diffusing among the several tribes, were deeply felt, were universally acknowledged; and a testimonial in the form of a statue or obelisk would have been immediately raised to his honor, in all parts of the land, had such been the fashion of the times. The brief but noble epitaph by the historian is, Joshua, "the servant of the Lord." <div eID="gen2949" type="x-p"/>
entries.334d46cb154405d705fe5af43314b210bd57ecb3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2194"/><div sID="gen2950" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2194"/><hi type="bold">31. Israel served the Lord all the days of Joshua--</hi>The high and commanding character of this eminent leader had given so decided a tone to the sentiments and manners of his contemporaries and the memory of his fervent piety and many virtues continued so vividly impressed on the memories of the people, that the sacred historian has recorded it to his immortal honor. "Israel served the Lord all the days of Joshua, and all the days of the elders that overlived Joshua." <div eID="gen2950" type="x-p"/>
entries.02fee061361ffb800d5891f982af439eb9570534: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2195"/><div sID="gen2951" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2195"/><hi type="bold">32. the bones of Joseph--</hi>They had carried these venerable relics with them in all their migrations through the desert, and deferred the burial, according to the dying charge of Joseph himself, till they arrived in the promised land. The sarcophagus, in which his mummied body had been put, was brought thither by the Israelites, and probably buried when the tribe of Ephraim had obtained their settlement, or at the solemn convocation described in this chapter.<div eID="gen2951" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2952" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in a parcel of ground which Jacob bought ... for an hundred pieces of silver--</hi>Kestitah translated, "piece of silver," is supposed to mean "a lamb," the weights being in the form of lambs or kids, which were, in all probability, the earliest standard of value among pastoral people. The tomb that now covers the spot is a Mohammedan Welce, but there is no reason to doubt that the precious deposit of Joseph's remains may be concealed there at the present time. <div eID="gen2952" type="x-p"/>
entries.d660fff5ec7efe844c855d77364520c1eef4dfeb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2196"/><div sID="gen2953" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2196"/><hi type="bold">33. Eleazar the son of Aaron died, and they buried him in ... mount Ephraim--</hi>The sepulchre is at the modern village Awertah, which, according to Jewish travellers, contains the graves also of Ithamar, the brother of Phinehas, the son of Eleazar [Van De Velde]. <chapter eID="Josh.24"/><div eID="gen2953" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen2606" osisID="Josh" type="book"/>

entries.b9b40a7807a73c8e238f8c3f7b7466cda13beaff: <div eID="gen8248" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen8249" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen8250" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen8250" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen8249" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen8251" type="x-p"/> Joshua gathers all the tribes together at Shechem, <reference osisRef="Jos.24.1">Jos 24:1</reference>; and gives them a history of God's gracious dealings with Abraham, <reference osisRef="Jos.24.2">Jos 24:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jos.24.3">Jos 24:3</reference>; Isaac, Jacob, and Esau, <reference osisRef="Jos.24.4">Jos 24:4</reference>; Moses and Aaron, and their fathers in Egypt, <reference osisRef="Jos.24.5">Jos 24:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jos.24.6">Jos 24:6</reference>. His judgments on the Egyptians, <reference osisRef="Jos.24.7">Jos 24:7</reference>. On the Amorites, <reference osisRef="Jos.24.8">Jos 24:8</reference>. Their deliverance from Balak and Balaam, <reference osisRef="Jos.24.9">Jos 24:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jos.24.10">Jos 24:10</reference>. Their conquests in the promised land, and their establishment in the possession of it, <reference osisRef="Jos.24.11-Jos.24.13">Jos 24:11-13</reference>. Exhorts them to abolish idolatry, and informs them of his and his family's resolution to serve Jehovah, <reference osisRef="Jos.24.14">Jos 24:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jos.24.15">Jos 24:15</reference>. The people solemnly promise to serve the Lord alone, and mention his merciful dealings towards them, <reference osisRef="Jos.24.16-Jos.24.18">Jos 24:16-18</reference>. Joshua shows them the holiness of God, and the danger of apostasy, <reference osisRef="Jos.24.19">Jos 24:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jos.24.20">Jos 24:20</reference>. The people again promise obedience, <reference osisRef="Jos.24.21">Jos 24:21</reference>. Joshua calls them to witness against themselves, that they had promised to worship God alone, and exhorts them to put away the strange gods, <reference osisRef="Jos.24.22">Jos 24:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jos.24.23">Jos 24:23</reference>. They promise obedience, <reference osisRef="Jos.24.24">Jos 24:24</reference>. Joshua makes a covenant with the people, writes it in a book, sets up a stone as a memorial of it, and dismisses the people, <reference osisRef="Jos.24.25-Jos.24.28">Jos 24:25-28</reference>. Joshua's death, <reference osisRef="Jos.24.29">Jos 24:29</reference>, and burial, <reference osisRef="Jos.24.30">Jos 24:30</reference>. The people continue faithful during that generation, <reference osisRef="Jos.24.31">Jos 24:31</reference>. They bury the bones of Joseph in Shechem, <reference osisRef="Jos.24.32">Jos 24:32</reference>. Eleazar the high priest dies also, <reference osisRef="Jos.24.33">Jos 24:33</reference>. <div eID="gen8251" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8252" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen8252" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8253" type="x-p"/> Joshua gathered all the tribes - This must have been a different assembly from that mentioned in the preceding chapter, though probably held not long after the former. <div eID="gen8253" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8254" type="x-p"/> To Shechem - As it is immediately added that they presented themselves before God, this must mean the tabernacle; but at this time the tabernacle was not at Shechem but at Shiloh. The Septuagint appear to have been struck with this difficulty, and therefore read Σηλω. Shiloh, both here and in <reference osisRef="Jos.24.25">Jos 24:25</reference>, though the Aldine and Complutensian editions have Συχεμ, Shechem, in both places. Many suppose that this is the original reading, and that Shechem has crept into the text instead of Shiloh. Perhaps there is more of imaginary than real difficulty in the text. As Joshua was now old and incapable of travelling, he certainly had a right to assemble the representatives of the tribes wherever he found most convenient, and to bring the ark of the covenant to the place of assembling: and this was probably done on this occasion. Shechem is a place famous in the patriarchal history. Here Abraham settled on his first coming into the land of Canaan, <reference osisRef="Gen.12.6">Gen 12:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.12.7">Gen 12:7</reference>; and here the patriarchs were buried, <reference osisRef="Act.7.16">Act 7:16</reference>. And as Shechem lay between Ebal and Gerizim, where Joshua had before made a covenant with the people, <reference osisRef="Jos.8.30">Jos 8:30</reference>, etc., the very circumstance of the place would be undoubtedly friendly to the solemnity of the present occasion. Shuckford supposes that the covenant was made at Shechem, and that the people went to Shiloh to confirm it before the Lord. Mr. Mede thinks the Ephraimites had a proseucha, or temporary oratory or house of prayer, at Shechem, whither the people resorted for Divine worship when they could not get to the tabernacle; and that this is what is called before the Lord; but this conjecture seems not at all likely, God having forbidden this kind of worship.
entries.e984cc084ad3e96bbb5d809775491235fc7d8166: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen8254" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8255" type="x-p"/> On the other side of the flood - The river Euphrates. <div eID="gen8255" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8256" type="x-p"/> They served other gods - Probably Abraham as well as Terah his father was an idolater, till he received the call of God to leave that land. See on <reference osisRef="Gen.11.31">Gen 11:31</reference> (note); <reference osisRef="Gen.12.1">Gen 12:1</reference> (note).
entries.9c43556e418f9e4740d322c73d3da37824ba492c: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen8256" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8257" type="x-p"/> Then Balak - arose and warred against Israel - This circumstance is not related in Numbers 22:1-41, nor does it appear in that history that the Moabites attacked the Israelites; and probably the warring here mentioned means no more than his attempts to destroy them by the curses of Balaam, and the wiles of the Midianitish women.
entries.1530873223c1a3f07fe4d33fd7bdfdc93f678aa2: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen8257" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8258" type="x-p"/> The men of Jericho fought against you - See the notes on Joshua 3:1-16 (note) and <reference osisRef="Jos.6.1">Jos 6:1</reference> (note), etc. The people of Jericho are said to have fought against the Israelites, because they opposed them by shutting their gates, etc., though they did not attempt to meet them in the field.
entries.8d913d30fcb0ea7802f89d92b134d03ec1d1bf24: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen8258" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8259" type="x-p"/> I sent the hornet before you - See the note on <reference osisRef="Exo.23.28">Exo 23:28</reference>.
entries.caf959a44dfc75d129e1e8c7f573041527755c3c: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen8259" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8260" type="x-p"/> Fear the Lord - Reverence him as the sole object of your religious worship. <div eID="gen8260" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8261" type="x-p"/> Serve him - Perform his will by obeying his commands. <div eID="gen8261" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8262" type="x-p"/> In sincerity - Having your whole heart engaged in his worship. <div eID="gen8262" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8263" type="x-p"/> And in truth - According to the directions he has given you in his infallible word. <div eID="gen8263" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8264" type="x-p"/> Put away the gods, etc. - From this exhortation of Joshua we learn of what sort the gods were, to the worship of whom these Israelites were still attached. <div eID="gen8264" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8265" type="x-p"/> 1. Those which their fathers worshipped on the other side of the flood: i.e., the gods of the Chaldeans, fire, light, the sun. <div eID="gen8265" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8266" type="x-p"/> 2. Those of the Egyptians, Apis, Anubis, the ape, serpents, vegetables, etc. <div eID="gen8266" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8267" type="x-p"/> 3. Those of the Canaanites, Moabites, etc., Baal-peor or Priapus, Astarte or Venus, etc., etc. <div eID="gen8267" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8268" type="x-p"/> All these he refers to in this and the following verse. See at the conclusion of <reference osisRef="Jos.24.33">Jos 24:33</reference> (note). How astonishing is this, that, after all God had done for them, and all the miracles they had seen, there should still be found among them both idols and idolaters! That it was so we have the fullest evidence, both here and in <reference osisRef="Jos.24.23">Jos 24:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amo.5.26">Amo 5:26</reference>; and in <reference osisRef="Act.7.41">Act 7:41</reference>. But what excuse can be made for such stupid, not to say brutish, blindness? Probably they thought they could the better represent the Divine nature by using symbols and images, and perhaps they professed to worship God through the medium of these. At least this is what has been alleged in behalf of a gross class of Christians who are notorious for image worship. But on such conduct God will never look with any allowance, where he has given his word and testimony.
entries.6f4f7afd62ee221940f713ed60abfa2280baee9e: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen8268" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8269" type="x-p"/> Choose you this day whom ye will serve - Joshua well knew that all service that was not free and voluntary could be only deceit and hypocrisy, and that God loveth a cheerful giver. He therefore calls upon the people to make their choice, for God himself would not force them - they must serve him with all their heart if they served him at all. As for himself and family, he shows them that their choice was already fixed, for they had taken Jehovah for their portion.
entries.c61e25f560e25e1e1db98c679ba392f0ed5444f2: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen8269" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8270" type="x-p"/> God forbid that we should forsake the Lord - That they were now sincere cannot be reasonably doubted, for they served the Lord all the days of Joshua, and the elders that outlived him, <reference osisRef="Jos.24.31">Jos 24:31</reference>; but afterwards they turned aside, and did serve other gods. "It is ordinary," says Mr. Trapp, "for the many-headed multitude to turn with the stream - to be of the same religion with their superiors: thus at Rome, in Diocletian's time, they were pagans; in Constantine's Christians; in Constantius's, Arians; in Julian's apostates, and in Jovinian's, Christians again! And all this within less than the age of a man. It is, therefore, a good thing that the heart be established with grace."
entries.e956e54350b5c479add1fcf5bf7b25ffce0993f3: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen8270" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8271" type="x-p"/> Ye cannot serve the Lord: for he is a holy God - If we are to take this literally, we cannot blame the Israelites for their defection from the worship of the true God; for if it was impossible for them to serve God, they could not but come short of his kingdom: but surely this was not the case. Instead of לא תוכלו lo thuchelu, ye Cannot serve, etc., some eminent critics read לא תכלו lo thechallu, ye shall not Cease to serve, etc. This is a very ingenious emendation, but there is not one MS. in all the collections of Kennicott and De Rossi to support it. However, it appears very possible that the first ו vau in תוכלו did not make a part of the word originally. If the common reading be preferred, the meaning of the place must be, "Ye cannot serve the Lord, for he is holy and jealous, unless ye put away the gods which your fathers served beyond the flood. For he is a jealous God, and will not give to nor divide his glory with any other. He is a holy God, and will not have his people defiled with the impure worship of the Gentiles."
entries.da508c9282f7e71272f436994908933890262592: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen8271" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8272" type="x-p"/> And the people said - Nay; but we will serve, etc. - So they understood the words of Joshua to imply no moral impossibility on their side: and had they earnestly sought the gracious assistance of God, they would have continued steady in his covenant.
entries.0e2475afa09ec4e308e26d123b8b2425e5c58d58: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen8272" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8273" type="x-p"/> Ye are witnesses against yourselves - Ye have been sufficiently apprised of the difficulties in your way - of God's holiness - your own weakness and inconstancy - the need you have of Divine help, and the awful consequences of apostasy; and now ye deliberately make your choice. Remember then, that ye are witnesses against yourselves, and your own conscience will be witness, judge, and executioner; or, as one terms it, index, judex, vindex.
entries.23389a2f91fe6c4e40f5d0e7c6eb87af86b1dbc7: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen8273" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8274" type="x-p"/> Now therefore put away - As you have promised to reform, begin instantly the work of reformation. A man's promise to serve God soon loses its moral hold of his conscience if he do not instantaneously begin to put it in practice. The grace that enables him to promise is that by the strength of which he is to begin the performance.
entries.f2923f7546fcd30fd2179132ab181fefc2eb92c9: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen8274" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8275" type="x-p"/> Joshua made a covenant - Literally, Joshua cut the covenant, alluding to the sacrifice offered on the occasion. <div eID="gen8275" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8276" type="x-p"/> And set then a statute and an ordinance - He made a solemn and public act of the whole, which was signed and witnessed by himself and the people, in the presence of Jehovah; and having done so, he wrote the words of the covenant in the book of the law of God, probably in some part of the skin constituting the great roll, on which the laws of God were written, and of which there were some blank columns to spare. Having done this, he took a great stone and set it up under an oak - that this might be עד ed or witness that, at such a time and place, this covenant was made, the terms of which might be found written in the book of the law, which was laid up beside the ark. See <reference osisRef="Deu.31.26">Deu 31:26</reference>.
entries.925b92a9c5ee403b6ff328f7037d5505d2f753a5: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen8276" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8277" type="x-p"/> This stone - hath heard all the words - That is, the stone itself, from its permanency, shall be in all succeeding ages as competent and as substantial a witness as one who had been present at the transaction, and heard all the words which on both sides were spoken on the occasion.
entries.fc1a1ad0d73fc82d905adde67df2a53d96d102cb: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen8277" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8278" type="x-p"/> So Joshua - After this verse the Septuagint insert <reference osisRef="Jos.24.31">Jos 24:31</reference>.
entries.b33d063b8ae9b64e064e0962614f67180f6d9944: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen8278" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8279" type="x-p"/> Joshua the son of Nun - died - This event probably took place shortly after this public assembly; for he was old and stricken in years when he held the assembly mentioned <reference osisRef="Jos.23.2">Jos 23:2</reference>; and as his work was now all done, and his soul ripened for a state of blessedness, God took him to himself, being one hundred and ten years of age; exactly the same age as that of the patriarch Joseph. See <reference osisRef="Gen.50.26">Gen 50:26</reference>.
entries.b8bbb322e7199ec2925c6d2c49ed541f8e4f06de: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen8279" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8280" type="x-p"/> And they buried him - in Timnath-serah - This was his own inheritance, as we have seen <reference osisRef="Jos.19.50">Jos 19:50</reference>. The Septuagint add here, "And they put with him there, in the tomb in which they buried him, the knives of stone with which he circumcised the children of Israel in Gilgal, according as the Lord commanded when he brought them out of Egypt; and there they are till this day." St. Augustine quotes the same passage in his thirtieth question on the book of Joshua, which, in all probability, he took from some copy of the Septuagint. It is very strange that there is no account of any public mourning for the death of this eminent general; probably, as he was buried in his own inheritance, he had forbidden all funeral pomp, and it is likely was privately interred.
entries.750417752aa06999a98a51f54e442ac529758154: <hi type="bold">Verse 31</hi> <div eID="gen8280" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8281" type="x-p"/> And Israel served the Lord, etc. - Though there was private idolatry among them, for they had strange gods, yet there was no public idolatry all the days of Joshua and of the elders that overlived Joshua; most of whom must have been advanced in years at the death of this great man. Hence Calmet supposes that the whole of this time might amount to about fifteen years. It has already been noted that this verse is placed by the Septuagint after <reference osisRef="Jos.24.28">Jos 24:28</reference>.
entries.328e7cfb44ef3dab902ccf75739e1d71c04c8b5e: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen8281" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8282" type="x-p"/> And the bones of Joseph - See the note on <reference osisRef="Gen.50.25">Gen 50:25</reference>, and on <reference osisRef="Exo.13.19">Exo 13:19</reference>. This burying of the bones of Joseph probably took place when the conquest of the land was completed, and each tribe had received its inheritance; for it is not likely that this was deferred till after the death of Joshua.
entries.4ae10929cd8db0c3221ef2dd962d7fd496338211: <hi type="bold">Verse 33</hi> <div eID="gen8282" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8283" type="x-p"/> And Eleazar - died - Probably about the same time as Joshua, or soon after; though some think he outlived him six years. Thus, nearly all the persons who had witnessed the miracles of God in the wilderness were gathered to their fathers; and their descendants left in possession of the great inheritance, with the Law of God in their hands, and the bright example of their illustrious ancestors before their eyes. It must be added that they possessed every advantage necessary to make them a great, a wise, and a holy people. How they used, or rather how they abused, these advantages, their subsequent history, given in the sacred books, amply testifies. <div eID="gen8283" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8284" type="x-p"/> A hill that pertained to Phinehas his son - This grant was probably made to Phinehas as a token of the respect of the whole nation, for his zeal, courage, and usefulness: for the priests had properly no inheritance. At the end of this verse the Septuagint add: - "In that day the children of Israel, taking up the ark of the covenant of God, carried it about with them, and Phinehas succeeded to the high priest's office in the place of his father until his death; and he was buried in Gabaath, which belonged to himself. "Then the children of Israel went every man to his own place, and to his own city. "And the children of Israel worshipped Astarte and Ashtaroth, and the gods of the surrounding nations, and the Lord delivered them into the hands of Eglon king of Moab, and he tyrannized over them for eighteen years." <div eID="gen8284" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8285" type="x-p"/> The last six verses in this chapter were, doubtless, not written by Joshua; for no man can give an account of his own death and burial. Eleazar, Phinehas, or Samuel, might have added them, to bring down the narration so as to connect it with their own times; and thus preserve the thread of the history unbroken. This is a common case; many men write histories of their own lives, which, in the last circumstances, are finished by others, and who has ever thought of impeaching the authenticity of the preceding part, because the subsequent was the work of a different hand? Hirtius's supplement has never invalidated the authenticity of the Commentaries of Caesar, nor the work of Quintus Smyrnaeus, that of the Iliad and Odyssey of Homer; nor the 13th book of Aeneid, by Mapheus Viggius, the authenticity of the preceding twelve, as the genuine work of Virgil. We should be thankful that an adequate and faithful hand has supplied those circumstances which the original author could not write, and without which the work would have been incomplete. Mr. Saurin has an excellent dissertation on this grand federal act formed by Joshua and the people of Israel on this very solemn occasion, of the substance of which the reader will not be displeased to find the following very short outline, which may be easily filled up by any whose business it is to instruct the public; for such a circumstance may with great propriety be brought before a Christian congregation at any time: - "Seven things are to be considered in this renewal of the covenant. <div eID="gen8285" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8286" type="x-p"/> I. The dignity of the mediator. <div eID="gen8286" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8287" type="x-p"/> II. The freedom of those who contracted. <div eID="gen8287" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8288" type="x-p"/> III. The necessity of the choice. <div eID="gen8288" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8289" type="x-p"/> IV. The extent of the conditions. <div eID="gen8289" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8290" type="x-p"/> V. The peril of the engagement. <div eID="gen8290" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8291" type="x-p"/> VI. The solemnity of the acceptance. <div eID="gen8291" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8292" type="x-p"/> VII. The nearness of the consequence. "I. The dignity of the mediator. - Take a view of his names, Hosea and Jehoshua. God will save: he will save. The first is like a promise; the second, the fulfillment of that promise. God will save some time or other: - this is the very person by whom he will accomplish his promise. Take a view of Joshua's life: his faith, courage, constancy, heroism, and success. A remarkable type of Christ. See <reference osisRef="Heb.4.8">Heb 4:8</reference>. "II. The freedom of those who contracted. - Take away the gods which your fathers served beyond the flood; and in Egypt, etc., <reference osisRef="Jos.24.14">Jos 24:14</reference>, etc. Joshua exhibits to the Israelites all the religions which were then known: <div eID="gen8292" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8293" type="x-p"/> 1. That of the Chaldeans, which consisted in the adoration of fire. <div eID="gen8293" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8294" type="x-p"/> 2. That of the Egyptians, which consisted in the worship of the ox Apis, cats, dogs, and serpents; which had been preceded by the worship even of vegetables, such as the onion, etc. <div eID="gen8294" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8295" type="x-p"/> 3. That of the people of Canaan, the principal objects of which were Astarte, (Venus), and Baal Peor, (Priapus). Make remarks on the liberty of choice which every man has, and which God, in matters of religion, applies to, and calls into action. "III. The necessity of the choice. - To be without religion, is to be without happiness here, and without any title to the kingdom of God. To have a false religion, is the broad road to perdition; and to have the true religion, and live agreeably to it, is the high road to heaven. Life is precarious - death is at the door - the Judge calls - much is to be done, and perhaps little time to do it in! Eternity depends on the present moment. Choose - choose speedily - determinately, etc. "IV. The extent of the conditions. - Fear the Lord, and serve him in truth and righteousness. Fear the Lord. Consider his being, his power, holiness, justice, etc. This is the gate to religion. Religion itself consists of two parts. <div eID="gen8295" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8296" type="x-p"/> I. Truth. <div eID="gen8296" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8297" type="x-p"/> 1. In opposition to the detestable idolatry of the forementioned nations. <div eID="gen8297" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8298" type="x-p"/> 2. In reference to that revelation which God gave of himself. <div eID="gen8298" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8299" type="x-p"/> 3. In reference to that solid peace and comfort which false religions may promise, but cannot give; and which the true religion communicates to all who properly embrace it. <div eID="gen8299" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8300" type="x-p"/> II. Uprightness or integrity, in opposition to those abominable vices by which themselves and the neighboring nations had been defiled. <div eID="gen8300" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8301" type="x-p"/> 1. The major part of men have one religion for youth, another for old age. But he who serves God in integrity, serves him with all his heart in every part of life. <div eID="gen8301" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8302" type="x-p"/> 2. Most men have a religion of times, places, and circumstances. This is a defective religion. Integrity takes in every time, every place, and every circumstance; God's law being ever kept before the eyes, and his love in the heart, dictating purity and perfection to every thought, word, and work. <div eID="gen8302" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8303" type="x-p"/> 3. Many content themselves with abstaining from vice, and think themselves sure of the kingdom of God because they do not sin as others. But he who serves God in integrity, not only abstains from the act and the appearance of evil, but steadily performs every moral good. <div eID="gen8303" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8304" type="x-p"/> 4. Many think that if they practice some kind of virtues, to which they feel less of a natural repugnance, they bid fair for the kingdom; but this is opposite to uprightness. The religion of God equally forbids every species of vice, and recommends every kind of virtue. "V. The peril of the engagement. - This covenant had in it the nature of an oath; for so much the phrase before the Lord implies: therefore those who entered into this covenant bound themselves by oath unto the Lord, to be steady and faithful in it.
